A cardiologist is a medical doctor who specializes in the heart and the network of blood vessels connected to it — the arteries, veins, and capillaries that carry blood throughout your body. Together, the heart and blood vessels form what is called the cardiovascular system, and that entire system is a cardiologist's area of expertise.
What exactly does a cardiologist do?

A cardiologist's job is to diagnose, treat, and prevent diseases and conditions that affect the heart and blood vessels. This includes things like:

  • Heart attacks — when blood flow to a part of the heart is blocked
  • Heart failure — when the heart can no longer pump blood efficiently
  • Irregular heartbeats (arrhythmias) — when the heart beats too fast, too slow, or in an unsteady rhythm
  • Blocked or narrowed arteries — which can starve the heart or other organs of blood
  • High blood pressure — which quietly damages the heart over time
  • Heart defects — structural problems with the heart, either present from birth or developed later
  • Valve problems — the heart has four valves that open and close to keep blood flowing in the right direction; these can become damaged or diseased

A cardiologist uses tools like ECGs (electrocardiograms), echocardiograms (ultrasound images of the heart), stress tests, and cardiac catheterization (inserting a thin tube into a blood vessel to examine the heart from the inside) to understand what is happening in a patient's heart.
Is a cardiologist the same as a heart surgeon?

No, and this distinction is important.

A cardiologist is not a surgeon. They manage heart conditions primarily through medicines, lifestyle advice, monitoring, and certain non-surgical procedures (like placing a stent — a small tube — to open a blocked artery, or implanting a pacemaker to regulate the heartbeat). These are called interventional or procedural treatments, but they are not open surgeries.

A cardiac surgeon (or cardiothoracic surgeon), on the other hand, actually opens the body to perform operations — such as bypass surgery, where new routes for blood flow are created around blocked arteries, or replacing a damaged heart valve. If a cardiologist determines that a patient needs surgery, they refer that patient to a cardiac surgeon.

Think of it this way: a cardiologist is like the doctor who deeply understands your heart problem and can fix many things without cutting you open, while a cardiac surgeon is the specialist brought in when cutting open is the only solution.
How is a cardiologist different from a regular doctor?

Your regular doctor — called a general practitioner (GP) or primary care physician — is trained to handle a wide range of health issues across the entire body. They are your first point of contact when something feels wrong.

A cardiologist is a specialist — someone who, after becoming a general doctor, spent many additional years studying only the heart and cardiovascular system. So if your GP notices something concerning about your heart, they will refer you to a cardiologist for a deeper, more expert evaluation.

Cardiology itself is a broad field, and some cardiologists focus on specific areas within it:

  • Interventional cardiologist — specializes in procedures like placing stents to open blocked arteries. They work a lot in the "cath lab" (catheterization laboratory).
  • Electrophysiologist — focuses specifically on the electrical system of the heart — the signals that tell your heart when to beat and at what rhythm. They treat arrhythmias and may implant pacemakers or perform ablations (where small areas of heart tissue causing electrical problems are intentionally destroyed).
  • Pediatric cardiologist — treats heart conditions specifically in babies, children, and teenagers, including congenital (present-from-birth) heart defects.
  • Preventive cardiologist — focuses on reducing the risk of heart disease before it develops, through managing cholesterol, blood pressure, diet, exercise, and genetics.
  • Heart failure specialist — manages patients whose hearts are weak and struggling to pump enough blood to meet the body's needs.
When would someone see a cardiologist?

You would be sent to (or choose to see) a cardiologist if you have symptoms or risk factors such as:

  • Chest pain or pressure
  • Shortness of breath, especially during mild activity or at rest
  • Palpitations (a fluttering or pounding sensation in your chest)
  • Fainting or dizziness
  • Swollen ankles or legs (which can signal fluid buildup from heart failure)
  • A family history of heart disease, especially at a young age
  • Abnormal results on a heart test done by your GP
  • Existing conditions like diabetes or high blood pressure that put stress on the heart over time
How does someone become a cardiologist?

Becoming a cardiologist requires a long and demanding path of education and training:

  1. Complete a medical degree (typically 4–5 years in most countries)
  2. Complete a residency in internal medicine (2–3 years of general hospital training)
  3. Complete a cardiology fellowship (3 or more additional years of specialized training focused purely on the heart)
  4. Pass licensing and specialty certification exams

In total, a cardiologist typically trains for 10–15 years after finishing school before they practice independently. This is why they are considered highly specialized and are consulted for complex heart-related matters.

A cardiologist is a highly trained specialist doctor whose entire focus is the health of the heart and blood vessels — diagnosing what goes wrong with them, treating those problems through medicines and non-surgical procedures, and helping patients prevent future heart disease.
